name: Wood vs. Faux Wood Blinds: Parkland or EverWood for Your Room?
heading: Wood vs. Faux Wood Blinds: Parkland or EverWood for Your Room?
title: Wood vs. Faux Wood Blinds | Parkland & EverWood
description: Compare Hunter Douglas Parkland wood blinds and EverWood faux wood blinds for finish, moisture exposure, light control and window fit.
excerpt: Compare Hunter Douglas Parkland wood blinds and EverWood faux wood blinds for finish, moisture exposure, light control and window fit.
author: John Crawford Company

cover.alt: Dark horizontal wood blinds across a bank of windows behind a white sofa.
cover.caption: Hunter Douglas Parkland® Wood Blinds

intro: Two white blinds can look similar from across a room. The decision between wood and faux wood becomes more useful when you consider what happens around the window: direct sun, bathroom humidity, nearby finishes and the way you open it each day.

Hunter Douglas Parkland Wood Blinds and EverWood Faux Wood Blinds offer different materials in a familiar horizontal style. Both let you tilt the slats for daylight and privacy. The choice begins with the room and the finish you want to see.

rows: Painted finishes or stains that show wood grain

table.caption: Parkland and EverWood at a glance

sections.heading: Start with the finish beside the window
paragraphs: Parkland is a natural starting point when visible wood grain is part of the look you want. Its stained finishes let the material contribute to the room alongside wood floors, furniture or trim. Painted wood is another option when you prefer a more uniform color.
EverWood provides a wood-style appearance in a different material. A painted look can coordinate across rooms even when exposure conditions lead you to use different products at different windows.

Compare finish samples with the surfaces that will stay in the room. A warm white blind can look different beside cooler white trim. For a stained blind, consider whether you want the wood tones to blend with your furniture or provide a deliberate contrast.

sections.heading: Treat moisture and sunlight as part of the product choice
paragraphs: A bathroom window and a living room window may need different materials. EverWood Faux Wood Blinds are designed to stand up to humidity and sunlight, with protection against fading, discoloration, warping and bowing. Those qualities make them worth comparing where moisture or strong sun affects the decision.

Tell us what the window is exposed to before settling on a finish. A room label alone does not explain the conditions: a kitchen window near steam can be different from one well away from the cooking area. We review the location and the product's suitability for it.

sections.heading: Slat size changes the appearance and the clearance
paragraphs: Both Parkland and EverWood offer 2-inch and 2½-inch slats. The broader slat changes the spacing you see when the blind is open and the horizontal pattern across the glass when it is closed.

The slats also need room to tilt. Window cranks, door handles and a shallow frame can affect how the blind is mounted. John Crawford Company measures the opening and checks those obstructions so the selection accounts for operation as well as appearance.

sections.heading: Decide whether you mostly tilt or fully raise the blind
paragraphs: Some people leave a blind lowered and adjust the slats as the light changes. Others raise it each morning to expose more glass. Think about your routine while comparing the controls and the fabric-free space you want at the window.

A raised horizontal blind leaves a stack of slats. Ask how that stack will sit at the top of your particular opening. For a bedroom, also discuss your expectations for darkness: closed slats reduce light, but gaps between slats and around the treatment can still admit it.

sections.heading: Choose for each room, then coordinate the result
paragraphs: Wood vs. faux wood blinds does not have to be a whole-house decision. Parkland may provide the grain you want in a sitting room, while EverWood suits the exposure in another space. Comparing the actual finishes helps keep those choices visually related.

John Crawford Company's blinds selection includes Hunter Douglas wood and faux wood options, with professional measuring and installation. Bring your room photos and finish ideas to an appointment at our Woodland Hills showroom, or arrange an in-home visit to compare samples where the blinds will be used.

name: Cellular Shades vs. Roller Shades: Duette or Designer Roller?
heading: Cellular Shades vs. Roller Shades: Duette or Designer Roller?
title: Cellular vs. Roller Shades | John Crawford Company
description: Compare Hunter Douglas Duette cellular shades and Designer Roller Shades for insulation, privacy, fabric choices and the fit at your windows.
excerpt: Compare Hunter Douglas Duette cellular shades and Designer Roller Shades for insulation, privacy, fabric choices and the fit at your windows.
author: John Crawford Company

cover.alt: Gray honeycomb shade across a wide bathroom window above a freestanding tub.
cover.caption: Hunter Douglas Duette® Honeycomb Shades

intro: Cellular shades are worth considering when you want added insulation at the window. Roller shades offer a flat fabric surface that can bring color, texture or pattern into the room. Both give you choices for managing daylight and privacy, but their construction changes how they look and operate.

For Hunter Douglas shoppers, that comparison often comes down to Duette Honeycomb Shades and Designer Roller Shades. Choosing between them gets easier when you look beyond the fabric sample and consider the shade fully lowered, partly open and raised.

sections.heading: What changes at the window?
paragraphs: A cellular shade has pleated fabric that forms pockets of air. A roller shade uses a continuous panel of fabric that wraps around a tube as it rises. Those differences remain visible as you use the shade throughout the day.

rows: A flat panel showing color, texture or pattern
A continuous fabric panel offers a simple appearance
table.caption: What changes at the window?

after: Neither style needs to be used throughout the entire house. A bedroom and a living room can call for different treatments, even when you want the rooms to feel connected.

sections.heading: Duette: consider comfort and flexible coverage
paragraphs: Duette Honeycomb Shades use a cellular structure that traps air within the fabric, adding insulation at the window. That construction deserves attention if the area beside your windows feels noticeably warmer or cooler than the rest of the room. The shade's fit and the window itself also affect comfort, so we consider the opening as part of the selection.
Duette shades have a pleated appearance when lowered. Look at that texture across the whole window, particularly if the room already has patterned upholstery, drapery or other fabrics.

Selected Duette configurations offer Top-Down/Bottom-Up operation. You can uncover glass at the top while keeping the lower portion covered, bringing daylight above eye level while maintaining coverage below. A window facing a walkway may benefit from that flexibility more than one overlooking a private garden.

sections.heading: Designer Roller: give the fabric a closer look
paragraphs: Designer Roller Shades offer fabrics ranging from sheer to opaque, with textures, prints and patterns. Because the lowered shade presents a flat area of fabric, the material has a strong influence on its appearance. A quiet neutral can sit alongside patterned furnishings. A more visible weave or print can make the window a feature of the room.
Compare samples with the shade lowered in mind. A small pattern that looks subtle in a sample book may become more noticeable across a broad window.
The finish at the top deserves attention, too. Discuss how the roll and selected hardware will look, especially if the shade will sit beneath existing drapery or within a shallow frame.

sections.heading: Separate daylight, privacy and bedroom darkness
paragraphs: When comparing cellular shades vs. roller shades, the fabric choice can matter as much as the style. For a living room, you may want daylight to pass through while reducing its intensity. For a bedroom, you may prefer substantially less light. At a window facing the street, your first concern may be privacy after dark.

Ask how the selected material behaves when the room is lit at night. Room-darkening fabric addresses light passing through the material; coverage around the opening also matters. A narrow band of light beside a shade can be noticeable in a bedroom even when the fabric itself blocks light well.

sections.heading: Look at the window with the shade raised
paragraphs: The shade's appearance when open is easy to overlook while choosing a color. Cellular fabric gathers as it rises, while roller fabric wraps around its tube. The amount of glass left exposed depends on the dimensions, construction and mounting position.

John Crawford Company checks frame depth, window handles and mounting space alongside width and height. If you prefer motorized operation, we also review the available controls for your chosen shade and window size. The product and the installation need to work together.

sections.heading: Compare the choices in your own room
paragraphs: Schedule an appointment at John Crawford Company's Woodland Hills showroom in Los Angeles, or request a free in-home consultation to compare suitable fabrics beside your windows. We help with shade selection, measuring and installation.

name: How to Choose Window Treatments for Large Windows
heading: How to Choose Window Treatments for Large Windows
title: Window Treatments for Large Windows | John Crawford
description: Compare shades, panels, drapery and controls for large windows. John Crawford Company explains light, privacy, fit and options for your home.
excerpt: Compare shade layouts, fabrics, side-to-side treatments and controls for wide windows, tall windows and walls of glass.
author: John Crawford Company

cover.alt: Pale screen shades across large living room windows overlooking the ocean.
cover.caption: Hunter Douglas Designer Screen Shades

intro: A wide living room window, a tall picture window and a wall of glass can each need a different approach. The right window treatment depends on the light coming in, the privacy you want and how you’d like to use the windows each day.

At John Crawford Company, we help you compare Hunter Douglas and Alta window treatments with those details in mind. Fabric and color are part of the choice. So are the arrangement, the controls and where the treatment will sit when it’s open.

sections.heading: Start with what you want to change about the room
paragraphs: Think about when your windows give you the most trouble. Afternoon sun might put glare across the television. A room that feels private during the day may feel exposed after dark. Or you may like the daylight and simply want to soften it.
Those situations call for different fabrics and levels of coverage.

If keeping the view is a priority, screen shades are worth considering. Their woven fabrics let you see through to varying degrees while filtering sunlight. Privacy changes with the lighting, though. When the room is lit at night, people outside may be able to see in. We’ll help you consider whether you need another layer for evening privacy.

For a bedroom, discuss how dark you want the room to feel. Light coming through the fabric and light entering around its edges are separate things. The mounting arrangement and coverage matter alongside the fabric you choose.

sections.heading: Compare one wide shade with several smaller shades
paragraphs: A large opening doesn’t always need one treatment across its entire width.

One wide shade gives you a continuous area of fabric. Several shades let you adjust different parts of the window separately. For example, you might lower the shade where the sun hits your seating area and leave the others open.

Window divisions can help guide the arrangement. On a row of three windows, individual shades may follow the frames naturally. Across one broad picture window, you’ll want to consider where the divisions between shades would fall.

Alta offers a two-on-one headrail arrangement for selected roller shades, allowing two shades to operate independently while sharing a continuous headrail. We can compare that approach with separate treatments and a single shade, depending on the opening and selected product.
Width, height, fabric and operating system all affect the available sizes. We check those details together when reviewing your windows.

sections.heading: Choose a treatment that suits the opening

subsections.heading: Roller and screen shades
paragraphs: Roller shades are a good starting point if you prefer a simple fabric treatment with little visual detail. Hunter Douglas Designer Roller Shades and Alta Roller Shades offer different fabrics and light-control choices.

Screen shades deserve a closer look when glare and the view are central to the decision. With a large area of glass, compare samples at the window so you can judge how clearly you can see outside and how much light comes through.

subsections.heading: Honeycomb shades
paragraphs: Honeycomb shades, also called cellular shades, are worth comparing when comfort is a concern. Their cellular construction traps air at the window, adding insulation.

Hunter Douglas Duette shades and Alta Honeycomb Shades offer different fabric and operating choices. We’ll help you compare the light control you want and the configurations available for your opening.

subsections.heading: Treatments that move from side to side
paragraphs: For a wide opening or sliding glass door, consider whether a treatment that travels sideways would be easier to use.

Hunter Douglas Luminette Sheer Panels combine sheer fabric with adjustable vertical vanes. Alta Panel Track shades use broad fabric panels that glide across the opening. They have different appearances and ways of controlling light, so seeing them operate can help you decide which you prefer.
If the opening includes a door, the treatment also needs to gather where it allows comfortable access.

sections.heading: Compare Hunter Douglas window treatments for large windows

rows.reason: A simple fabric treatment that keeps the window’s appearance uncluttered.
rows.light: Fabrics range from sheer to opaque, with different levels of light control and privacy.
rows.planning: Compare one wide shade with several smaller shades. Consider light entering around the fabric’s edges.

rows.reason: Controlling glare while keeping a view outside.
rows.light: Fabric openness affects visibility and light control. View-through fabrics may need another layer for nighttime privacy.
rows.planning: Compare samples at the window to judge the view and privacy you’ll have.

rows.reason: Adding insulation at a large area of glass.
rows.light: Light-filtering and room-darkening fabric choices suit different rooms.
rows.planning: Compare the shade’s pleated appearance and how much glass it covers when raised. Selected configurations also open sideways for doors.

rows.reason: A soft, drapery-like appearance across wide windows or sliding doors.
rows.light: Rotating fabric vanes let you adjust light and privacy while the sheer fabric softens daylight.
rows.planning: Allow space for the treatment to gather at the side when open.

rows.reason: Broad fabric panels with a contemporary look for wide or tall openings.
rows.light: Fabric opacity determines how much light comes through and how much privacy the panels provide.
rows.planning: Panels glide sideways and stack together. Their resting position should work with the view, furniture and door access.

sections.note: Available sizes, fabrics and controls vary by configuration. We’ll measure your opening and help you compare the combinations that fit your windows.

sections.heading: Look at the window treatment when it’s open
paragraphs: It’s easy to focus on how a treatment looks across the glass. Give some attention to where it goes when you open it.
A raised shade occupies space at the top of the window. Drapery and sliding panels gather at the sides. The amount of space they use affects how much glass remains visible.

With drapery, we look at the rod or track, the fabric fullness and where the panels will rest. Stationary side panels can frame the window, while a shade handles the everyday light control. Curtains that close across the opening need their own allowance for coverage and movement.
Window depth, handles, trim and nearby furniture also affect the fit. These details are part of measuring for the complete treatment.

sections.heading: Choose controls you’ll be comfortable using
paragraphs: Large windows often put controls out of easy reach, especially behind furniture or above a stairway.

Motorized operation lets you adjust compatible treatments without reaching each window. We work with Hunter Douglas PowerView and Somfy systems, and can explain the controls available with the shades you’re considering.

Power deserves attention too. With a rechargeable system, consider how you’ll reach the charging connection. For a hardwired installation, the power connection needs to be coordinated with the selected system. We’ll talk through those requirements as part of the product choice.

sections.heading: Compare samples beside your own windows
paragraphs: A fabric sample can look different against a bright window than it does on a table. Seeing it in your room helps you judge the color, texture and light coming through it.
During a free in-home consultation, we bring samples, take measurements and help you compare suitable options within your budget. You can also arrange an appointment at our Woodland Hills showroom.
